title: The DARK Truth About Women on Old West Stagecoaches (The Movies Never Showed This)
fullText: Hollywood showed the elegant lady stepping down from the stage coach with a parasol and a smile, a lie. The reality of the women who crossed the West in stage coaches was documented by the women themselves in diaries, letters, [music] and testimonies that stayed tucked away for decades. What they wrote about those journeys is hard to read. Watch until the end. Number 21 is the most disturbing. Number one, on old west stage coaches, there were no scheduled bathroom stops. When nature called, the men would just get out or use a bucket right there. But for women, it was a very different story. Imagine trying to deal with that while wearing layer upon layer of clothing, a tight corset, and those huge hoop frames under the skirt. In practice, it was impossible. And what did many of them do? They stopped drinking water days before boarding. Days. On a trip that could last weeks under the blazing sun and constant dust, the result was predictable. Urinary tract infections, kidney problems, and severe dehydration became common among female passengers. Nobody talked about it at the time. It was considered improper. But medical records tell a different story. one that shows the real price these women's bodies paid just to make the journey. Number two, women traveled in tight corsets because society expected them to. Now imagine wearing one of those corsets inside a stage coach with no suspension, getting slammed around in potholes for 12 hours straight. The result was brutal. Frontier doctors like George Holiday documented cases of broken ribs, fainting from lack of air, and even internal bleeding in female passengers. The corset squeezed the chest tightly, and every jolt in the road worked like a blow against ribs that were already under pressure. Many women arrived at their destination in worse shape than any cowboy injured on horseback. And the worst part was taking the corset off was not an option. A woman without a corset in public was seen as indecent. So they endured it in silence. In [music] this case, the road was not what did the most damage. It was the social code no one questioned. Number three, stage coaches were built to hold nine passengers, but in practice they crammed in as many as 15. Imagine a woman back then, raised never to touch a man who was not a relative, being squeezed between two strangers for hours on end. The seats had no separation at all, and your knees would end up tangled with the knees of the person in front of you. Every hole in the road threw everyone into each other. Diaries from the time reveal that many women pretended to sleep through the entire trip just to avoid conversation and eye contact. Others cried quietly without being able to complain because there simply was no alternative. Some even paid double the fair, trying to secure a window seat, which at least gave them one free side. The detail few people tell is that many men took advantage of those jolts on purpose [music] and nobody said a word. Number four, harassment did not even have a name yet. Back then, the word did not exist, but the behavior was routine. Inside a cramped stage coach where strangers were packed together for days, women dealt with hands that accidentally brushed against them in the dark. Indecent whispers and comments about their bodies made like jokes in front of everyone. Diaries from women who traveled across the West [music] described situations that today anyone would recognize immediately. But back then, if a woman complained, she was called hysterical or ill-mannered. Silence was the only option considered respectable. And the worst part, the drivers rarely stepped in because they did not want to lose paying passengers. So women learned to endure it in silence, gritting their teeth until the next stop. Number five, pregnant women traveled in those stage coaches because they simply had no other choice. Soldiers, wives following their husbands, settler women heading to new territories. The problem is that nobody talked about what happened to them during the trip. The constant shaking caused miscarriages and that is not speculation. It is documented in records from the transportation companies themselves [music] and in letters from the time. Some women went into labor right there inside the coach in the middle of the road with no doctor, nothing. The other female passengers did what they could, improvising as midwives. Babies were still born. Mothers did not survive childbirth, and the stage coach did not stop. The driver had a schedule to keep, and neither birth nor death was reason enough to delay the route. Number six, think about this. A 25-day trip squeezed onto a wooden seat with strangers beside you. Now, imagine going through that while on your period with no disposable products because they simply did not exist. Women [music] used strips of cotton that had to be washed and reused, but washed where? Dried how? There was no extra clean water and not a single moment of privacy. The result was predictable. Infections became routine on those journeys. And the most revealing part is the silence. No men's diaries from that time mention this subject. The ones written by women, when they dare to mention it, use coded language and disguised phrases. A kind of suffering that happened every month in front of everyone. And that history treated as if it had never existed. Number seven. When a man died in some remote town out west, his widow faced a problem few people imagine. There were no trains on much of the route, so the only way to take the body back to the family in the east was on the stage coach itself. The woman paid an extra fair for the coffin, which was tied to the roof or wedged in among the luggage. In some cases, the body even rode inside the coach right next to the passengers. Imagine the scene. A grieving woman stuck for days in a cramped space, surrounded by strangers who could barely hide their discomfort. The smell got worse at every stop. Nobody offered condolences because nobody knew what to say. Her grief did not get a single moment of silence or privacy. It was public, dragged out, and stripped of any dignity. and she still had to keep her composure because any open display of pain made the other passengers uncomfortable. Number eight, small towns in the west had a serious problem. They did not have enough female teachers. The solution was to recruit single women from the east, often through newspaper ads. They accepted the job, packed up their things, and set off alone on a stage coach to places they had never seen before. The trip lasted for weeks through lawless territory. The disturbing detail is that their destination was public information. Everyone knew where they were going. Drivers, passengers, people at the stage stops. Some of those women simply never made it to their final destination. And the contracts those towns offered said nothing about what would happen if the teacher disappeared along the way. There was no protocol, no organized search. If she vanished, they hired another one. It was as if the risk of the journey was entirely her problem. Number nine. In the 1900s, cities like Chicago and Pittsburgh tried to ban long hat pins. Why? Because women were using those accessories, some up to 10 in long, as weapons to defend themselves against abusive men. But that practice [music] did not start on the streets of big cities. Decades earlier, inside stage coaches, women were already hiding those pins as their only real protection against male passengers who tried to grab them in the cramped seats. With no sheriff around and no room to get away, the hatpin was what they had. And it worked. One stab to the arm or the face quickly handled what words could not. The most striking part is that nobody questioned [music] the hatpin when it was only being used for fashion. The problem started when women began fighting back. That is when politicians wanted to ban it. The tool was the same. What changed was who got to decide how to use it. Number 10. A woman traveling alone on a stage coach carried an invisible burden. Without a man by her side, she automatically became suspicious. Station owners treated that passenger like someone of questionable morals, a runaway, or even a prostitute. And that changed everything. Her food came last. The room she was given was the worst one available. and the other passengers felt free to make comments they never would have made in front of a husband. Many women quickly learned to protect themselves with a simple lie. They said their husband was waiting at the next stop. Some even carried fake wedding rings just to avoid trouble. It was not vanity. It was survival. Because back then a woman traveling alone was not seen as independent. She was seen as available. And that rule was not written down anywhere, but everyone followed it. Number 11. In records left by Old West travelers, there are accounts of women who went into labor inside moving stage coaches. In one of those stories, a passenger described in her diary how another woman gave birth right there in the cramped cabin with strangers all around her. The baby was born alive. The driver stopped for less than an hour. After that, the trip went on. The mother, still bleeding, was left at the next station with the baby in her arms. No doctor, no guaranteed help. The most disturbing part is the silence that came afterward. No official record mentions that woman's name. No one wrote down whether she survived or what happened to the child. To the stage coach companies, it was just an unscheduled stop. 40 minutes behind schedule, nothing more. Number 12. When outlaws or native warriors attacked a stage coach, the passengers fate was divided in a brutal way. Men were usually killed right there or left behind with nothing. But young women often faced a different end. They were taken. It was not the exception. It was the pattern. Cynthia Anne Parker was captured at the age of nine in 1836 and lived for decades among the Comanche. But her case became famous precisely because there were dozens of others no one remembers. Women captured along the routes out west simply disappeared from the records. And here is the detail most people do not know. The stage coach companies themselves knew about that risk. They had internal reports about earlier attacks and they knew which stretches were the most dangerous. Even so, they sold tickets to women traveling alone without giving any warning at all. Profit came first. The passenger's safety was her own problem. Number [music] 13. On long stage coach trips, stops were rare and decided by the driver, not the passengers. When the vehicle finally did stop, the scene was always the same. An open stretch of land with no facilities, not enough bushes, nothing. The men would simply walk a few yards away and take care of their business without a second thought. For women, the situation was completely different. They came up with their own system of protection. They formed a tight circle, lifted their full skirts like makeshift curtains, and took turns in the middle. One protected the other with her own body. That gesture shows up again and again in diaries from the time as the only real moment of female solidarity during the entire trip. Some women reported going all day without drinking water just to avoid that exposure, which led to frequent fainting spells [music] on the hottest stretches. Number 14. Imagine wearing the same clothes for an entire week in 104° heat without bathing even once. That was exactly what women dealt with on stage coaches. They traveled in heavy dresses, [music] tight corsets, multiple layers of petticoats, and leather boots, and they could not change out of any of it. The reason was simple. The coach was cramped and shared with strangers, men and women sitting side by side. There was no curtain, no stop with a restroom, no privacy at all. Sweat built up under all those layers, and their skin started to suffer. Chafing showed up in the first few days. Then came open soores, infections that spread and could become genuinely dangerous. And the worst part is that nobody talked about it. They just endured it in silence because complaining was not an option back then. Number 15. The stations along the routes were places to switch horses and grab a quick rest. But for women traveling alone, they posed a real danger. These stops were in remote areas run by men who lived in isolation for months, many of them with questionable backgrounds and easy access to alcohol. There was no oversight, no law nearby. Accounts from the time show that many female passengers preferred to spend the night inside the stage coach itself, sitting cramped and uncomfortable, rather than accept a room at those stations. And here is a detail few people know. The Butterfield Overland Mail even circulated informal guidance recommending that women simply not get off at certain points along the route. In other words, the company itself knew about the danger and instead of fixing the problem, it merely suggested that female passengers avoid certain places. That says a lot about how women's protection worked in the Old West. Number 16. [music] Many soldiers wives faced a situation few people stopped to think about. The husband would be transferred to some isolated fort deep in wild territory and send a letter asking her to come join him. The problem was that the letter could take weeks or even months to arrive. In that gap, anything could happen. Attacks, disease, accidents. The woman would gather the little she had, pay for a stage coach ticket, and face weeks of brutal travel with no idea what she would find at the end. There was no telegraph at many of those forts. There was no way to confirm anything. And when she finally arrived exhausted and broke, sometimes she was told that her husband had already been buried weeks earlier with no money to go back, no one she knew, [music] and nowhere to go. The stage coach fair was expensive and only covered one leg of the trip. She was stranded in a place she had never chosen, number 17. Here's something not many people stopped to think about. In the Old West, a woman inside a stage coach could be in pain, hungry, burning up from the heat, or terrified. And even then, she was expected to stay quiet. Complaining was seen as weakness, a lack of composure. Society at the time treated women's suffering as something they were supposed to swallow in silence. And the most striking part is [music] this. When you read these women's diaries written in private just for themselves, many of them still apologized for being tired. They felt guilty for feeling what any human being would have felt under those conditions. That self-imposed silence helps explain why these stories stayed buried for so long. No one told them because women were trained not to tell them. Number 18. There was a phenomenon that doctors at the time could barely explain. They called it prairie madness. Weeks confined in a cramped space, barely sleeping, going through things no one should have to go through. It broke the minds of many women. Some arrived at their destination unable to speak. Others screamed nonstop. And the worst [music] part was that nobody treated it like an illness. The solution was simple and cruel. They locked these women in a back room at some boarding house or sent them back to their families as if they were damaged goods. Asylums in the West had wards full of women who arrived that way by stage coach. In the records, there was only a cold note, disturbed upon arrival. No doctor's name, no diagnosis, no plan for recovery. Number 19. Many women kept diaries during the trip, but what they wrote there was not just simple descriptions of the scenery. They developed their own language full of abbreviations and vague phrases that hid harsh truths. A note like, "A visit from Mr. M could mean harassment. Indis disposition was a common code for an unwanted pregnancy or a miscarriage. Historian Lillian Schlissell spent years analyzing these diaries in women's diaries of the westward journey and [music] noticed the same patterns showing up in dozens of different accounts. These were not isolated cases. It was a silent system of recordkeeping that let women document abuse without exposing themselves to the judgment of husbands, pastors, or neighbors. They knew no one would protect them, so they created their own archive of the truth hidden in plain sight. Number 20. Many women wrote letters during stage coach stops. They poured out everything, the fear, the discomfort, the humiliating situations they faced on the road. But when they reached their [music] destination, they kept those letters and never sent them. They were too honest. Decades later, historians found those folded papers inside trunks, hidden among old clothes and personal belongings in attics. They were letters to mothers, sisters, childhood friends. In them, these women described things they never would have dared to say out loud at the time. Some told stories so harsh they even apologized for writing them. These documents became some of the most direct and unfiltered records to survive from that period. No history book from that time tells what those letters tell. Number 21. Katherine H's diary written in 1849 during the gold rush was forgotten for decades. In it, she described in detail what women went through on those crossings, illness, childbirth on the trail, harassment from fellow travelers, and brutal decisions about who got left behind. Publishers refused the text in the late 19th century, claiming the content was inappropriate for women readers of the time. Her family kept the manuscript for generations. It was not until the 20th century that historians finally published it, revealing names, dates, and places the official version had always preferred to ignore. What she recorded did not fit the myth of the heroic West that Hollywood liked to sell. And maybe that is exactly why it was silenced for so long. The question that remains is simple. How many other diaries like this are still sitting in some basement waiting for someone brave enough to open

segments.viText: Nó được công khai, lôi ra và tước bỏ mọi phẩm giá.

segments.text: and she still had to keep her composure because any open display of pain made the other passengers uncomfortable.
segments.viText: và cô vẫn phải giữ bình tĩnh vì bất kỳ biểu hiện đau đớn nào cũng khiến những hành khách khác khó chịu.

segments.text: Number eight, small towns in the west had a serious problem.
segments.viText: Thứ tám, các thị trấn nhỏ ở phía Tây đang gặp vấn đề nghiêm trọng.

segments.text: They did not have enough female teachers.
segments.viText: Họ không có đủ giáo viên nữ.

segments.text: The solution was to recruit single women from the east, often through newspaper ads.
segments.viText: Giải pháp là tuyển dụng những phụ nữ độc thân từ miền đông, thường thông qua quảng cáo trên báo.

segments.text: They accepted the job, packed up their things, and set off alone on a stage coach to places they had never seen before.
segments.viText: Họ nhận lời, thu dọn đồ đạc và một mình lên xe ngựa đến những nơi mà họ chưa từng thấy trước đây.

segments.text: The trip lasted for weeks through lawless territory.
segments.viText: Chuyến đi kéo dài hàng tuần qua lãnh thổ vô luật pháp.

segments.text: The disturbing detail is that their destination was public information.
segments.viText: Chi tiết đáng lo ngại là đích đến của họ là thông tin công khai.

segments.text: Everyone knew where they were going.
segments.viText: Mọi người đều biết họ sẽ đi đâu.

segments.text: Drivers, passengers, people at the stage stops.
segments.viText: Lái xe, hành khách, người dân ở sân khấu dừng lại.

segments.text: Some of those women simply never made it to their final destination.
segments.viText: Một số phụ nữ đó đơn giản là không bao giờ đến được đích cuối cùng.

segments.text: And the contracts those towns offered said nothing about what would happen if the teacher disappeared along the way.
segments.viText: Và những hợp đồng mà các thị trấn đưa ra không nói gì về điều gì sẽ xảy ra nếu giáo viên biến mất trên đường đi.

segments.text: There was no protocol, no organized search.
segments.viText: Không có giao thức, không có tìm kiếm có tổ chức.

segments.text: If she vanished, they hired another one.
segments.viText: Nếu cô ấy biến mất, họ sẽ thuê một người khác.

segments.text: It was as if the risk of the journey was entirely her problem.
segments.viText: Cứ như thể sự mạo hiểm của cuộc hành trình hoàn toàn là vấn đề của cô.

segments.text: Number nine.
segments.viText: Số chín.

segments.text: In the 1900s, cities like Chicago and Pittsburgh tried to ban long hat pins.
segments.viText: Vào những năm 1900, các thành phố như Chicago và Pittsburgh đã cố gắng cấm ghim cài mũ dài.

segments.text: Why?
segments.viText: Why?

segments.text: Because women were using those accessories, some up to 10 in long, as weapons to defend themselves against abusive men.
segments.viText: Bởi vì phụ nữ sử dụng những phụ kiện đó, có những chiếc dài tới 10 chiếc, làm vũ khí để tự vệ trước những người đàn ông bạo hành.

segments.text: But that practice [music] did not start on the streets of big cities.
segments.viText: Nhưng [âm nhạc] đó không bắt đầu trên đường phố của các thành phố lớn.

segments.text: Decades earlier, inside stage coaches, women were already hiding those pins as their only real protection against male passengers who tried to grab them in the cramped seats.
segments.viText: Nhiều thập kỷ trước, bên trong các toa xe sân khấu, phụ nữ đã giấu những chiếc ghim đó như một biện pháp bảo vệ thực sự duy nhất của họ trước những hành khách nam cố gắng tóm lấy họ trên những chiếc ghế chật chội.

segments.text: With no sheriff around and no room to get away, the hatpin was what they had.
segments.viText: Không có cảnh sát trưởng xung quanh và không có chỗ để trốn thoát, chiếc kẹp mũ là thứ họ có.

segments.text: And it worked.
segments.viText: Và nó đã hoạt động.

segments.text: One stab to the arm or the face quickly handled what words could not.
segments.viText: Một cú đâm vào tay hay vào mặt sẽ nhanh chóng xử lý được điều mà lời nói không thể xử lý được.

segments.text: The most striking part is that nobody questioned [music] the hatpin when it was only being used for fashion.
segments.viText: Điều nổi bật nhất là không ai thắc mắc về [âm nhạc] chiếc kẹp mũ khi nó chỉ được sử dụng cho thời trang.

segments.text: The problem started when women began fighting back.
segments.viText: Vấn đề bắt đầu khi phụ nữ bắt đầu chống trả.

segments.text: That is when politicians wanted to ban it.
segments.viText: Đó là lúc các chính trị gia muốn cấm nó.

segments.text: The tool was the same.
segments.viText: Công cụ này giống nhau.

segments.text: What changed was who got to decide how to use it.
segments.viText: Điều thay đổi là ai có quyền quyết định cách sử dụng nó.

segments.text: Number 10.
segments.viText: Số 10.

segments.text: A woman traveling alone on a stage coach carried an invisible burden.
segments.viText: Một người phụ nữ đi một mình trên cỗ xe sân khấu mang theo một gánh nặng vô hình.

segments.text: Without a man by her side, she automatically became suspicious.
segments.viText: Không có người đàn ông bên cạnh, cô tự động trở nên nghi ngờ.

segments.text: Station owners treated that passenger like someone of questionable morals, a runaway, or even a prostitute.
segments.viText: Các chủ nhà ga đối xử với hành khách đó như một người có vấn đề về đạo đức, một kẻ bỏ trốn hoặc thậm chí là một gái mại dâm.

segments.text: And that changed everything.
segments.viText: Và điều đó đã thay đổi mọi thứ.

segments.text: Her food came last.
segments.viText: Thức ăn của cô ấy đến sau cùng.

segments.text: The room she was given was the worst one available.
segments.viText: Căn phòng cô được cho là căn phòng tồi tệ nhất.

segments.text: and the other passengers felt free to make comments they never would have made in front of a husband.
segments.viText: và những hành khách khác thoải mái đưa ra những nhận xét mà họ chưa bao giờ đưa ra trước mặt một người chồng.

segments.text: Many women quickly learned to protect themselves with a simple lie.
segments.viText: Nhiều phụ nữ nhanh chóng học cách tự bảo vệ mình bằng một lời nói dối đơn giản.

segments.text: They said their husband was waiting at the next stop.
segments.viText: Họ nói chồng họ đang đợi ở điểm dừng tiếp theo.

segments.text: Some even carried fake wedding rings just to avoid trouble.
segments.viText: Một số thậm chí còn mang theo nhẫn cưới giả chỉ để tránh rắc rối.

segments.text: It was not vanity.
segments.viText: Đó không phải là sự phù phiếm.

segments.text: It was survival.
segments.viText: Đó là sự sống còn.

segments.text: Because back then a woman traveling alone was not seen as independent.
segments.viText: Bởi vì thời đó phụ nữ đi du lịch một mình không được coi là độc lập.

segments.text: She was seen as available.
segments.viText: Cô ấy được coi là có sẵn.

segments.text: And that rule was not written down anywhere, but everyone followed it.
segments.viText: Và quy tắc đó không được viết ra ở bất cứ đâu mà mọi người đều tuân theo.

segments.text: Number 11.
segments.viText: Số 11.

segments.text: In records left by Old West travelers, there are accounts of women who went into labor inside moving stage coaches.
segments.viText: Trong hồ sơ do những người du hành Old West để lại, có lời kể về những phụ nữ đã chuyển dạ bên trong những chiếc xe ngựa đang di chuyển.

segments.text: In one of those stories, a passenger described in her diary how another woman gave birth right there in the cramped cabin with strangers all around her.
segments.viText: Trong một trong những câu chuyện đó, một hành khách đã mô tả trong nhật ký của mình về việc một người phụ nữ khác đã sinh con ngay trong cabin chật chội với những người lạ vây quanh cô ấy.

segments.text: The baby was born alive.
segments.viText: Đứa bé được sinh ra còn sống.

segments.text: The driver stopped for less than an hour.
segments.viText: Người lái xe dừng lại chưa đầy một giờ.

segments.text: After that, the trip went on.
segments.viText: Sau đó, chuyến đi lại tiếp tục.

segments.text: The mother, still bleeding, was left at the next station with the baby in her arms.
segments.viText: Người mẹ vẫn đang chảy máu, bị bỏ lại ở ga tiếp theo với đứa bé trên tay.

segments.text: No doctor, no guaranteed help.
segments.viText: Không có bác sĩ, không có sự giúp đỡ đảm bảo.

segments.text: The most disturbing part is the silence that came afterward.
segments.viText: Điều đáng lo ngại nhất là sự im lặng sau đó.

segments.text: No official record mentions that woman's name.
segments.viText: Không có hồ sơ chính thức nào đề cập đến tên của người phụ nữ đó.

segments.text: No one wrote down whether she survived or what happened to the child.
segments.viText: Không ai viết lại liệu cô ấy có sống sót hay điều gì đã xảy ra với đứa trẻ.

segments.text: To the stage coach companies, it was just an unscheduled stop.
segments.viText: Đối với các hãng xe sân khấu, đó chỉ là một điểm dừng đột xuất.

segments.text: 40 minutes behind schedule, nothing more.
segments.viText: Chậm 40 phút so với lịch trình, không có gì hơn.

segments.text: Number 12.
segments.viText: Số 12.

segments.text: When outlaws or native warriors attacked a stage coach, the passengers fate was divided in a brutal way.
segments.viText: Khi những kẻ ngoài vòng pháp luật hoặc các chiến binh bản địa tấn công một huấn luyện viên sân khấu, số phận của hành khách bị chia cắt một cách tàn bạo.

segments.text: Men were usually killed right there or left behind with nothing.
segments.viText: Đàn ông thường bị giết ngay tại đó hoặc không bị bỏ lại gì.

segments.text: But young women often faced a different end.
segments.viText: Nhưng những phụ nữ trẻ thường phải đối mặt với một kết cục khác.

segments.text: They were taken.
segments.viText: Họ đã bị bắt.

segments.text: It was not the exception.
segments.viText: Đó không phải là ngoại lệ.

segments.text: It was the pattern.
segments.viText: Đó là mô hình.

segments.text: Cynthia Anne Parker was captured at the age of nine in 1836 and lived for decades among the Comanche.
segments.viText: Cynthia Anne Parker bị bắt khi mới 9 tuổi vào năm 1836 và sống hàng thập kỷ giữa người Comanche.

segments.text: But her case became famous precisely because there were dozens of others no one remembers.
segments.viText: Nhưng trường hợp của cô trở nên nổi tiếng chính vì có hàng tá trường hợp khác không ai nhớ đến.

segments.text: Women captured along the routes out west simply disappeared from the records.
segments.viText: Những phụ nữ bị bắt dọc theo các tuyến đường về phía tây đơn giản biến mất khỏi hồ sơ.

segments.text: And here is the detail most people do not know.
segments.viText: Và đây là chi tiết mà hầu hết mọi người không biết.

segments.text: The stage coach companies themselves knew about that risk.
segments.viText: Bản thân các công ty huấn luyện viên sân khấu cũng biết trước rủi ro đó.

segments.text: They had internal reports about earlier attacks and they knew which stretches were the most dangerous.
segments.viText: Họ đã có báo cáo nội bộ về các cuộc tấn công trước đó và họ biết đoạn đường nào là nguy hiểm nhất.

segments.text: Even so, they sold tickets to women traveling alone without giving any warning at all.
segments.viText: Mặc dù vậy, họ vẫn bán vé cho phụ nữ đi một mình mà không đưa ra bất kỳ lời cảnh báo nào.

segments.text: Profit came first.
segments.viText: Lợi nhuận đến trước.

segments.text: The passenger's safety was her own problem.
segments.viText: Sự an toàn của hành khách là vấn đề của riêng cô.

segments.text: Number [music] 13.
segments.viText: Số [âm nhạc] 13.

segments.text: On long stage coach trips, stops were rare and decided by the driver, not the passengers.
segments.viText: Trong các chuyến xe khách chặng dài, hiếm khi có điểm dừng và do người lái xe quyết định chứ không phải hành khách.

segments.text: When the vehicle finally did stop, the scene was always the same.
segments.viText: Khi chiếc xe cuối cùng đã dừng lại, khung cảnh vẫn như cũ.

segments.text: An open stretch of land with no facilities, not enough bushes, nothing.
segments.viText: Một dải đất trống không có cơ sở vật chất, không đủ cây bụi, không có gì.

segments.text: The men would simply walk a few yards away and take care of their business without a second thought.
segments.viText: Những người đàn ông chỉ cần đi bộ vài mét và lo công việc kinh doanh của họ mà không cần suy nghĩ kỹ.

segments.text: For women, the situation was completely different.
segments.viText: Đối với phụ nữ, tình hình hoàn toàn khác.

segments.text: They came up with their own system of protection.
segments.viText: Họ đã nghĩ ra hệ thống bảo vệ của riêng mình.

segments.text: They formed a tight circle, lifted their full skirts like makeshift curtains, and took turns in the middle.
segments.viText: Họ tạo thành một vòng tròn chặt chẽ, vén váy dài lên như những tấm màn tạm bợ và thay phiên nhau đứng ở giữa.

segments.text: One protected the other with her own body.
segments.viText: Một người bảo vệ người kia bằng chính cơ thể của mình.

segments.text: That gesture shows up again and again in diaries from the time as the only real moment of female solidarity during the entire trip.
segments.viText: Cử chỉ đó xuất hiện lặp đi lặp lại trong nhật ký từ thời đó như khoảnh khắc thực sự duy nhất của tình đoàn kết phụ nữ trong suốt chuyến đi.

segments.text: Some women reported going all day without drinking water just to avoid that exposure, which led to frequent fainting spells [music] on the hottest stretches.
segments.viText: Một số phụ nữ cho biết họ phải đi cả ngày mà không uống nước chỉ để tránh bị phơi nhiễm, điều này dẫn đến việc thường xuyên ngất xỉu [âm nhạc] trong những khoảng thời gian nóng nhất.

segments.text: Number 14.
segments.viText: Số 14.

segments.text: Imagine wearing the same clothes for an entire week in 104° heat without bathing even once.
segments.viText: Hãy tưởng tượng mặc cùng một bộ quần áo trong cả tuần dưới cái nóng 104° mà không tắm dù chỉ một lần.

segments.text: That was exactly what women dealt with on stage coaches.
segments.viText: Đó chính xác là những gì phụ nữ phải đối mặt trên sân khấu.

segments.text: They traveled in heavy dresses, [music] tight corsets, multiple layers of petticoats, and leather boots, and they could not change out of any of it.
segments.viText: Họ đi du lịch trong những bộ váy nặng nề, áo nịt ngực bó sát [âm nhạc], nhiều lớp váy lót và ủng da, và họ không thể thay bất cứ thứ gì trong số đó.

segments.text: The reason was simple.
segments.viText: Lý do rất đơn giản.

segments.text: The coach was cramped and shared with strangers, men and women sitting side by side.
segments.viText: Xe chật chội, chia sẻ với người lạ, nam nữ ngồi cạnh nhau.

segments.text: There was no curtain, no stop with a restroom, no privacy at all.
segments.viText: Không có rèm che, không có nhà vệ sinh, không có sự riêng tư nào cả.

segments.text: Sweat built up under all those layers, and their skin started to suffer.
segments.viText: Mồ hôi tích tụ dưới những lớp đó và làn da của họ bắt đầu đau khổ.

segments.text: Chafing showed up in the first few days.
segments.viText: Chafing xuất hiện trong vài ngày đầu tiên.

segments.text: Then came open soores, infections that spread and could become genuinely dangerous.
segments.viText: Sau đó xuất hiện các vết loét hở, nhiễm trùng lan rộng và có thể trở nên thực sự nguy hiểm.

segments.text: And the worst part is that nobody talked about it.
segments.viText: Và điều tệ nhất là không ai nói về nó.

segments.text: They just endured it in silence because complaining was not an option back then.
segments.viText: Họ chỉ im lặng chịu đựng vì lúc đó phàn nàn không phải là một lựa chọn.

segments.text: Number 15.
segments.viText: Số 15.

segments.text: The stations along the routes were places to switch horses and grab a quick rest.
segments.viText: Các trạm dọc tuyến đường là nơi đổi ngựa và nghỉ ngơi nhanh chóng.

segments.text: But for women traveling alone, they posed a real danger.
segments.viText: Nhưng đối với phụ nữ đi du lịch một mình, chúng thực sự là một mối nguy hiểm.

segments.text: These stops were in remote areas run by men who lived in isolation for months, many of them with questionable backgrounds and easy access to alcohol.
segments.viText: Những điểm dừng này nằm ở những khu vực hẻo lánh do những người đàn ông sống cô lập trong nhiều tháng điều hành, nhiều người trong số họ có lý lịch đáng ngờ và dễ dàng tiếp cận với rượu.

segments.text: There was no oversight, no law nearby.
segments.viText: Không có sự giám sát, không có luật pháp gần đó.

segments.text: Accounts from the time show that many female passengers preferred to spend the night inside the stage coach itself, sitting cramped and uncomfortable, rather than accept a room at those stations.
segments.viText: Các tài khoản vào thời điểm đó cho thấy nhiều hành khách nữ thích qua đêm bên trong toa xe, ngồi chật chội và không thoải mái hơn là nhận phòng tại các nhà ga đó.

segments.text: And here is a detail few people know.
segments.viText: Và đây là một chi tiết ít người biết.

segments.text: The Butterfield Overland Mail even circulated informal guidance recommending that women simply not get off at certain points along the route.
segments.viText: Butterfield Overland Mail thậm chí còn lưu hành hướng dẫn không chính thức khuyến nghị phụ nữ không nên xuống xe tại một số điểm nhất định dọc tuyến đường.

segments.text: In other words, the company itself knew about the danger and instead of fixing the problem, it merely suggested that female passengers avoid certain places.
segments.viText: Nói cách khác, bản thân công ty cũng biết về mối nguy hiểm và thay vì khắc phục sự cố, họ chỉ đề nghị hành khách nữ tránh một số địa điểm nhất định.

segments.text: That says a lot about how women's protection worked in the Old West.
segments.viText: Điều đó nói lên nhiều điều về cách thức hoạt động của cơ chế bảo vệ phụ nữ ở Phương Tây Cổ.

segments.text: Number 16.
segments.viText: Số 16.

segments.text: [music] Many soldiers wives faced a situation few people stopped to think about.
segments.viText: [âm nhạc] Vợ của nhiều người lính phải đối mặt với một tình huống mà ít người dừng lại để suy nghĩ.

segments.text: The husband would be transferred to some isolated fort deep in wild territory and send a letter asking her to come join him.
segments.viText: Người chồng sẽ được chuyển đến một pháo đài biệt lập nào đó sâu trong lãnh thổ hoang dã và gửi một lá thư mời cô đến tham gia cùng anh ta.

segments.text: The problem was that the letter could take weeks or even months to arrive.
segments.viText: Vấn đề là lá thư có thể phải mất hàng tuần, thậm chí hàng tháng mới đến nơi.

segments.text: In that gap, anything could happen.
segments.viText: Trong khoảng trống đó, bất cứ điều gì có thể xảy ra.

segments.text: Attacks, disease, accidents.
segments.viText: Tấn công, bệnh tật, tai nạn.

segments.text: The woman would gather the little she had, pay for a stage coach ticket, and face weeks of brutal travel with no idea what she would find at the end.
segments.viText: Người phụ nữ sẽ thu thập số tiền ít ỏi mình có, trả tiền mua vé xe ngựa sân khấu và đối mặt với nhiều tuần di chuyển khắc nghiệt mà không biết cuối cùng mình sẽ tìm thấy điều gì.

segments.text: There was no telegraph at many of those forts.
segments.viText: Không có điện báo ở nhiều pháo đài đó.

segments.text: There was no way to confirm anything.
segments.viText: Không có cách nào để xác nhận bất cứ điều gì.

segments.text: And when she finally arrived exhausted and broke, sometimes she was told that her husband had already been buried weeks earlier with no money to go back, no one she knew, [music] and nowhere to go.
segments.viText: Và cuối cùng khi cô ấy đến nơi, kiệt sức và suy sụp, đôi khi cô ấy được thông báo rằng chồng cô ấy đã được chôn cất nhiều tuần trước đó mà không có tiền để về, không ai quen biết, [âm nhạc] và không nơi nào để đi.

segments.text: The stage coach fair was expensive and only covered one leg of the trip.
segments.viText: Hội chợ xe sân khấu rất tốn kém và chỉ bao gồm một chặng của chuyến đi.

segments.text: She was stranded in a place she had never chosen, number 17.
segments.viText: Cô bị mắc kẹt ở một nơi mà cô chưa bao giờ chọn, số 17.

segments.text: Here's something not many people stopped to think about.
segments.viText: Đây là điều mà không nhiều người dừng lại để suy nghĩ.

segments.text: In the Old West, a woman inside a stage coach could be in pain, hungry, burning up from the heat, or terrified.
segments.viText: Ở phương Tây cổ, một người phụ nữ ngồi trong xe sân khấu có thể bị đau, đói, nóng bừng người hoặc sợ hãi.

segments.text: And even then, she was expected to stay quiet.
segments.viText: Và ngay cả khi đó, cô ấy vẫn phải giữ im lặng.

segments.text: Complaining was seen as weakness, a lack of composure.
segments.viText: Phàn nàn bị coi là sự yếu đuối, thiếu bình tĩnh.

segments.text: Society at the time treated women's suffering as something they were supposed to swallow in silence.
segments.viText: Xã hội thời đó coi nỗi đau khổ của phụ nữ là thứ họ phải nuốt chửng trong im lặng.

segments.text: And the most striking part is [music] this.
segments.viText: Và phần nổi bật nhất là [âm nhạc] này.

segments.text: When you read these women's diaries written in private just for themselves, many of them still apologized for being tired.
segments.viText: Khi đọc nhật ký của những người phụ nữ này viết riêng cho mình, nhiều người trong số họ vẫn xin lỗi vì mệt mỏi.

segments.text: They felt guilty for feeling what any human being would have felt under those conditions.
segments.viText: Họ cảm thấy tội lỗi vì đã cảm thấy những gì mà bất kỳ con người nào cũng sẽ cảm thấy trong những điều kiện đó.

segments.text: That self-imposed silence helps explain why these stories stayed buried for so long.
segments.viText: Sự im lặng tự áp đặt đó giúp giải thích tại sao những câu chuyện này lại bị chôn vùi lâu đến vậy.

segments.text: No one told them because women were trained not to tell them.
segments.viText: Không ai nói với họ vì phụ nữ được huấn luyện để không nói với họ.

segments.text: Number 18.
segments.viText: Số 18.

segments.text: There was a phenomenon that doctors at the time could barely explain.
segments.viText: Có một hiện tượng mà các bác sĩ thời đó khó có thể giải thích được.

segments.text: They called it prairie madness.
segments.viText: Họ gọi đó là sự điên rồ của thảo nguyên.

segments.text: Weeks confined in a cramped space, barely sleeping, going through things no one should have to go through.
segments.viText: Nhiều tuần bị giam cầm trong không gian chật chội, hầu như không ngủ, trải qua những điều lẽ ra không ai phải trải qua.

segments.text: It broke the minds of many women.
segments.viText: Nó đã làm tan nát tâm trí của nhiều phụ nữ.

segments.text: Some arrived at their destination unable to speak.
segments.viText: Một số đến nơi không thể nói được.

segments.text: Others screamed nonstop.
segments.viText: Những người khác la hét không ngừng.

segments.text: And the worst [music] part was that nobody treated it like an illness.
segments.viText: Và phần [âm nhạc] tệ nhất là không ai coi nó như một căn bệnh.

segments.text: The solution was simple and cruel.
segments.viText: Giải pháp rất đơn giản và tàn nhẫn.

segments.text: They locked these women in a back room at some boarding house or sent them back to their families as if they were damaged goods.
segments.viText: Họ nhốt những người phụ nữ này vào phòng sau của một nhà trọ nào đó hoặc gửi về gia đình như đồ hư hỏng.

segments.text: Asylums in the West had wards full of women who arrived that way by stage coach.
segments.viText: Các trại tị nạn ở phương Tây có những khu đầy phụ nữ đến bằng xe ngựa sân khấu.

segments.text: In the records, there was only a cold note, disturbed upon arrival.
segments.viText: Trong hồ sơ chỉ có một tờ giấy lạnh, bị xáo trộn khi đến nơi.

segments.text: No doctor's name, no diagnosis, no plan for recovery.
segments.viText: Không tên bác sĩ, không chẩn đoán, không kế hoạch phục hồi.

segments.text: Number 19.
segments.viText: Số 19.

segments.text: Many women kept diaries during the trip, but what they wrote there was not just simple descriptions of the scenery.
segments.viText: Nhiều phụ nữ đã ghi nhật ký trong suốt chuyến đi, nhưng những gì họ viết trong đó không chỉ là những mô tả đơn giản về phong cảnh.

segments.text: They developed their own language full of abbreviations and vague phrases that hid harsh truths.
segments.viText: Họ đã phát triển ngôn ngữ riêng của mình với đầy những chữ viết tắt và những cụm từ mơ hồ che giấu những sự thật phũ phàng.

segments.text: A note like, "A visit from Mr.
segments.viText: Một ghi chú như "Một chuyến thăm của ông

segments.text: M could mean harassment.
segments.viText: M có thể có nghĩa là quấy rối.

segments.text: Indis disposition was a common code for an unwanted pregnancy or a miscarriage.
segments.viText: Tính cách của người Ấn Độ là dấu hiệu phổ biến cho việc mang thai ngoài ý muốn hoặc sẩy thai.

segments.text: Historian Lillian Schlissell spent years analyzing these diaries in women's diaries of the westward journey and [music] noticed the same patterns showing up in dozens of different accounts.
segments.viText: Nhà sử học Lillian Schlissell đã dành nhiều năm để phân tích những cuốn nhật ký này trong nhật ký của phụ nữ trong chuyến hành trình về phía Tây và [âm nhạc] nhận thấy những khuôn mẫu tương tự xuất hiện trong hàng chục câu chuyện khác nhau.

segments.text: These were not isolated cases.
segments.viText: Đây không phải là những trường hợp cá biệt.

segments.text: It was a silent system of recordkeeping that let women document abuse without exposing themselves to the judgment of husbands, pastors, or neighbors.
segments.viText: Đó là một hệ thống lưu trữ hồ sơ im lặng cho phép phụ nữ ghi lại hành vi lạm dụng mà không phải chịu sự phán xét của chồng, mục sư hoặc hàng xóm.

segments.text: They knew no one would protect them, so they created their own archive of the truth hidden in plain sight.
segments.viText: Họ biết sẽ không có ai bảo vệ họ, vì vậy họ đã tạo ra kho lưu trữ sự thật của riêng mình được giấu kín trong tầm nhìn rõ ràng.

segments.text: Number 20.
segments.viText: Số 20.

segments.text: Many women wrote letters during stage coach stops.
segments.viText: Nhiều phụ nữ đã viết thư trong lúc xe ngựa dừng lại.

segments.text: They poured out everything, the fear, the discomfort, the humiliating situations they faced on the road.
segments.viText: Họ trút hết mọi thứ, nỗi sợ hãi, sự khó chịu, những tình huống nhục nhã mà họ gặp phải trên đường.

segments.text: But when they reached their [music] destination, they kept those letters and never sent them.
segments.viText: Nhưng khi đến nơi [âm nhạc], họ giữ lại những bức thư đó và không bao giờ gửi chúng đi.

segments.text: They were too honest.
segments.viText: Họ đã quá trung thực.

segments.text: Decades later, historians found those folded papers inside trunks, hidden among old clothes and personal belongings in attics.
segments.viText: Nhiều thập kỷ sau, các nhà sử học đã tìm thấy những tờ giấy gấp đó bên trong những chiếc rương, giấu trong quần áo cũ và đồ dùng cá nhân trên gác mái.

segments.text: They were letters to mothers, sisters, childhood friends.
segments.viText: Đó là những lá thư gửi mẹ, chị, bạn thời thơ ấu.

segments.text: In them, these women described things they never would have dared to say out loud at the time.
segments.viText: Trong đó, những người phụ nữ này mô tả những điều mà họ chưa bao giờ dám nói thành tiếng vào thời điểm đó.

segments.text: Some told stories so harsh they even apologized for writing them.
segments.viText: Một số người kể những câu chuyện gay gắt đến mức họ thậm chí còn xin lỗi vì đã viết chúng.

segments.text: These documents became some of the most direct and unfiltered records to survive from that period.
segments.viText: Những tài liệu này đã trở thành một trong những hồ sơ trực tiếp và chưa được lọc nhất để tồn tại từ thời kỳ đó.

segments.text: No history book from that time tells what those letters tell.
segments.viText: Không có cuốn sách lịch sử nào từ thời đó kể lại những gì những lá thư đó kể.

segments.text: Number 21.
segments.viText: Số 21.

segments.text: Katherine H's diary written in 1849 during the gold rush was forgotten for decades.
segments.viText: Nhật ký của Katherine H viết năm 1849 trong cơn sốt vàng đã bị lãng quên trong nhiều thập kỷ.

segments.text: In it, she described in detail what women went through on those crossings, illness, childbirth on the trail, harassment from fellow travelers, and brutal decisions about who got left behind.
segments.viText: Trong đó, cô mô tả chi tiết những gì phụ nữ đã trải qua trong những chuyến vượt biển đó, bệnh tật, sinh con trên đường mòn, sự quấy rối từ những người bạn đồng hành và những quyết định tàn bạo về những người bị bỏ lại phía sau.

segments.text: Publishers refused the text in the late 19th century, claiming the content was inappropriate for women readers of the time.
segments.viText: Các nhà xuất bản đã từ chối văn bản này vào cuối thế kỷ 19, cho rằng nội dung này không phù hợp với độc giả nữ thời đó.

segments.text: Her family kept the manuscript for generations.
segments.viText: Gia đình bà đã lưu giữ bản thảo qua nhiều thế hệ.

segments.text: It was not until the 20th century that historians finally published it, revealing names, dates, and places the official version had always preferred to ignore.
segments.viText: Mãi đến thế kỷ 20, các nhà sử học cuối cùng mới công bố nó, tiết lộ tên, ngày tháng và địa điểm mà phiên bản chính thức luôn muốn bỏ qua.

segments.text: What she recorded did not fit the myth of the heroic West that Hollywood liked to sell.
segments.viText: Những gì cô ghi lại không phù hợp với huyền thoại về miền Tây anh hùng mà Hollywood thích rao bán.

segments.text: And maybe that is exactly why it was silenced for so long.
segments.viText: Và có lẽ đó chính xác là lý do tại sao nó lại im lặng lâu đến vậy.

segments.text: The question that remains is simple.
segments.viText: Câu hỏi còn lại rất đơn giản.

segments.viText: Còn bao nhiêu cuốn nhật ký như thế này vẫn đang ngồi dưới tầng hầm nào đó chờ ai đó đủ dũng cảm mở ra
